propositions.text: Dismiss the appeal and find the Appellant has a viable IFA in Nairobi or Mombasa.
propositions.quote: I dismiss this appeal. XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Kenya who is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated March 19, 2018, rejecting her claim for refugee protection on the basis that she has an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Nairobi or Mombasa.

propositions.text: Appellant fears domestic violence and forced FGM by her husband if returned to Kenya.
propositions.quote: She fears that if she returns to Kenya her husband will subject her to domestic violence and force her and their children to undergo Female Genital Mutilation (FGM).

propositions.text: Appellant asks RAD to substitute RPD decision for positive one or refer back for redetermination.
propositions.quote: She is asking the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to substitute the RPD determination for a positive one, or in the alternative, refer this matter back to the RPD for redetermination.

propositions.text: Appellant submitted new evidence and requested oral hearing.
propositions.quote: She has submitted new evidence and requested an oral hearing.

propositions.text: Accept some new evidence but reject request for oral hearing.
propositions.quote: I have accepted some of this new evidence but rejected the request for an oral hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal, finds a viable IFA, notes appellant's fears, her requests for substitution or redetermination, new evidence, and rejects oral hearing.

propositions.text: Dismiss appeal and confirm RPD decision that Appellant is not a refugee or person in need of protection under IRPA.
propositions.quote: I dismiss her appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention1 refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

propositions.text: Appellant could live safely in Nairobi or Mombasa and relocation would not be objectively unreasonable.
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant could live safely in Nairobi or Mombasa and that this relocation would not be objectively unreasonable for her.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal, confirms RPD decision, and finds safe, reasonable relocation to Nairobi or Mombasa.

propositions.text: Only some of the evidence presented by the Appellant is accepted.
propositions.quote: Only some of the evidence presented by the Appellant is accepted.

paragraphs.summary: The court accepts only some of the appellant's evidence.

propositions.text: New evidence was challenging to assess due to some not new, missing info, unclear sources, minimal argument on criteria.
propositions.quote: the new evidence submitted for this appeal was challenging to assess as some of this evidence is not new as it was previously before the RPD, some of the exhibits presented as new evidence had information missing, the source of the information was unclear for some documents and there is minimal argument as to how the evidence presented meets the required criteria.

propositions.text: Appellant sought to enter 17 items of new evidence including articles, reports, photos, and BOC form.
propositions.quote: the following documentation was sought by the Appellant to be entered as new evidence: 1) A Wikipedia article on female genital mutilation of unknown date; 2) NYT article on FGM dated January 13, 2018; 3) Guardian article on FGM in Kenya dated December 23, 2016; 4) a document called "The challenge of eradicating FGM" of unknown date and unknown source; 5) a series of pages which appear to be related to "FGM/Plan International" of unknown date; 6) a document called "This practice should be stopped" dated January 22, 2018; 7) a document called "Female Genital Mutilation: Kenya's worst-kept secret" dated February 16, 2017 from the Daily Maverick; 8) a document called "Female Genital Mutilation in Kenya" dated September 21, 2015; 9) a document called "FGM among the Maasai community of Kenya dated March 8, 2005 of unclear source; 10) Al Jazeera article titled "Magazine: A Witness to FGM" dated July 10, 2015; 11) Reuters article titled "Kenyan doctor goes to court to legalize female genital mutilation" dated January 19, 2018; 12) a medical report dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018; 13) Appellant's CV letter from XXXX XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 2018; 14) photos of unknown date and unknown persons with the Appellant; 15) photos of unknown date with the Appellant alone or with unknown persons; 16) a medical letter dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018; and, 17) the Appellant's Basis of Claim (BOC) form.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds new evidence challenging to assess and lists 17 items appellant sought to enter.

propositions.text: Only evidence that arose after RPD decision, was not reasonably available, or could not reasonably have been brought before RPD can be accepted.
propositions.quote: According to the law,3 I can only accept evidence that: i. arose after the RPD decision; ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the legal criteria for accepting new evidence on appeal.

propositions.text: Evidence must be new, credible and relevant to be accepted.
propositions.quote: If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.

paragraphs.summary: The court states evidence must be new, credible, and relevant to be accepted.

propositions.text: Appellant's explanation that former Counsel was inexperienced is inadequate to meet new evidence criteria.
propositions.quote: I do not find this explanation adequate or sufficient to address how the Appellant's new evidence meets the strict requirements.

propositions.text: Appellant argues former Counsel was inexperienced and failed to provide sufficient evidence to RPD.
propositions.quote: the only reason that I can locate regarding how the new evidence meets these criteria is that the Appellant's former Counsel was not experienced and failed to provided sufficient and satisfactory evidence to the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects appellant's argument that former Counsel's inexperience justifies new evidence acceptance.

propositions.text: Decline to accept items #1 through #11 as they were reasonably available to Appellant before RPD.
propositions.quote: I decline to accept items #1 through #11 as I find that all these documents were reasonably available to the Appellant to present to the RPD.

propositions.text: Appellant's general assertion about Counsel's inexperience is inadequate to explain failure to present these publicly available documents.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's general assertion that her past Counsel was not experienced is inadequate to explain why all of these items, which are all readily and publicly available, could not have been presented to the RPD.

propositions.text: No evidence of formal complaint against past Counsel.
propositions.quote: There is no evidence before me to indicate that a formal complaint has been launched against the Appellant's past Counsel.

paragraphs.summary: The court declines items #1-11, finds them reasonably available, and rejects counsel inexperience as explanation.

propositions.text: Decline to enter item #12 (medical report) as irrelevant to IFA issue.
propositions.quote: I decline to enter item #12 which is a Canadian medical report relating to the Appellant's left knee ultrasound as I find that this document has no relevance to the determinative issue in this appeal, which is the viability of an IFA in Kenya.

propositions.text: No submission on how item #12 meets required criteria.
propositions.quote: Again, I note that there is no submission as to how this document meets the required criteria.

paragraphs.summary: The court declines item #12 as irrelevant and notes no submission on criteria.

propositions.text: Decline to enter items #14 and #15 (photos) as irrelevant and unexplained significance.
propositions.quote: Items #14 and #15, which represent pictures of an unknown date which appear to be the Appellant with unknown persons, I also decline to enter as new evidence as I find that this evidence is not relevant to the determinative issue of IFA.

propositions.text: No explanation why photos were not provided to RPD.
propositions.quote: There is also no explanation provided to me as to the significance of these pictures and why these pictures were not provided to the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court declines photos #14 and #15 as irrelevant and unexplained.

propositions.text: Decline to enter item #17 (BOC form) as it is already in RPD record and not new evidence.
propositions.quote: The last item, #17 which is the Appellant's BOC form, I decline to enter as this is in the RPD Record and is not new evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court declines item #17 as it is not new evidence.

propositions.text: Accept only items #13 (CV letter) and #18 (medical letter) as new evidence relevant to IFA assessment.
propositions.quote: The only evidence I will accept for this appeal is item #13 (Appellant's CV letter from XXXX 2018) and item #18 (medical letter relating to an assessment and report conducted in XXXX 2018), as I find that these two documents arose after the RPD decision and have relevancy in my assessment of the reasonableness of an IFA for the Appellant in Kenya.

paragraphs.summary: The court accepts only items #13 and #18 as new relevant evidence.

propositions.text: Further evidence submitted after perfection was confusing and included two documents: a 2018 report and a Canadian church support letter.
propositions.quote: Further evidence was submitted to the RAD subsequent to perfection of the appeal. I also found this application confusing as the same argument regarding the inadequacy of the Appellant's Counsel before the RPD was advanced as the reason why this evidence could not be submitted. Further, the evidence to be entered under RAD Rule 29 was not readily found with the application. Despite these challenges, I believe that the only documents which the Appellant sought to enter under RAD Rule 29 included: 1) a report dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 20187 from Dr. XXXX; and 2) a support letter from a Canadian church dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 20188.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds further evidence submitted after perfection confusing, listing two documents sought to be entered.

propositions.text: RAD Rule 29 governs use of documents not previously provided, requiring application and consideration of relevance, new evidence, and effort to provide earlier.
propositions.quote: As this evidence was submitted following perfection, I must consider this "new" evidence, pursuant to RAD Rule 29: Documents or written submissions not previously provided - person 29 (1) A person who is the subject of an appeal who does not provide a document or written submissions with the appellant's record, respondent's record or reply record must not use the document or provide the written submissions in the appeal unless allowed to do so by the Division. Application (2) If a person who is the subject of an appeal wants to use a document or provide written submissions that were not previously provided, the person must make an application to the Division in accordance with rule 37. Documents - new evidence (3) The person who is the subject of the appeal must include in an application to use a document that was not previously provided an explanation of how the document meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Act and how that evidence relates to the person, unless the document is being presented in response to evidence presented by the Minister. Factors (4) In deciding whether to allow an application, the Division must consider any relevant factors, including (a) the document's relevance and probative value; (b) any new evidence the document brings to the appeal; and (c) whether the person who is the subject of the appeal, with reasonable effort, could have provided the document or written submissions with the appellant's record, respondent's record or reply record.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains RAD Rule 29 requirements for new evidence submitted after perfection.

propositions.text: Cases Semykina and Arisekola require considering Singh and Raza factors even if section 110(4) would reject evidence.
propositions.quote: In assessing the proposed new evidence in the RAD Rule 29 application, I also note the cases of Semykina9and Arisekola10 which state that unlike section110(4)11 applications, even if a proposed document would otherwise be rejected under the statutory requirements of section110(4), the Singh12 and Raza13 factors must still be considered.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes case law requires considering Singh and Raza factors for RAD Rule 29 evidence.

propositions.text: Enter 2018 report as evidence due to assessor availability issues and relevance to IFA.
propositions.quote: I will enter into evidence the report dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 as I have accepted the Appellant's explanation that there were issues with assessor availability and the time required to complete the report. I find the report to have some relevance to my IFA analysis.

propositions.text: Do not enter Canadian church support letter as no explanation for late submission and no relevance to IFA.
propositions.quote: I will not enter into evidence the support letter from a Canadian church as there is no explanation provided as to why such a letter could not have been provided to the RPD or with the perfection of this appeal. I also find that the content within this letter is not relevant to the determinative issue in this appeal which is the viability of an IFA for the Appellant in Kenya.

paragraphs.summary: The court admits the 2018 report but rejects the Canadian church letter for lack of explanation and relevance.

propositions.text: Deny oral hearing request as new evidence does not raise credibility issues.
propositions.quote: While I did accept some new evidence, I find that this evidence does not raise a credibility issue or concern. Accordingly, I am unable to hold an oral hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court denies oral hearing as new evidence does not raise credibility concerns.

propositions.text: Court's role is to review all evidence and decide if RPD decision was correct.
propositions.quote: My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.

propositions.text: Considered all evidence including RPD hearing transcript and Gender Guidelines.
propositions.quote: In making this assessment, I have considered all the evidence, including the written transcript of the RPD hearing, as well as the Chairperson Guidelines 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution (Gender Guidelines).

propositions.text: Determinative issue is viability of an IFA, which will be the focus.
propositions.quote: I find that the determinative issue in this appeal relates to the viability of an IFA, so this will be my focus.

paragraphs.summary: The court states its role, evidence considered, and that the key issue is viability of an IFA.

propositions.text: IFA test requires no serious risk of persecution or torture and that relocation is not unreasonable for claimant.
propositions.quote: The test to apply in order to determine whether a viable IFA exists is two-pronged and requires that the RPD find, on a balance of probabilities, that: (i) there is no serious possibility of the Claimant being persecuted or subjected, on a balance of probabilities, to a danger of torture or to a risk to their life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the proposed IFA area; and, (ii) conditions in the IFA area must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the Claimant, for the Claimant to seek refuge there.

propositions.text: The threshold for the unreasonable test is very high.
propositions.quote: The threshold is very high for the unreasonable test.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the two-pronged IFA test and that the unreasonable test threshold is very high.

propositions.text: Mombasa and Nairobi were proposed as IFAs at RPD hearing start.
propositions.quote: Mombasa and Nairobi were proposed as a possible IFAs at the start of the RPD hearing.

propositions.text: Appellant testified husband would search everywhere and track her via phone or school database.
propositions.quote: The Appellant testified that her husband was motivated to search for her and her daughters everywhere in Kenya and would be capable of tracking her through her mobile phone or the school registration data base.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Mombasa and Nairobi as proposed IFAs; appellant testified husband would track her everywhere.

propositions.text: Consider if the Appellant's husband is motivated and capable of locating her in IFA locations Mombasa or Nairobi.
propositions.quote: In considering the forward-facing risk of harm that the Appellant might face in the IFA locations of Mombasa or Nairobi, I have considered whether the agent of persecution (which is the Appellant's husband in this case) is motivated and capable of locating the Appellant in these IFA locations.

paragraphs.summary: The court considers whether the Appellant's husband is motivated and capable of locating her in the IFA locations of Mombasa or Nairobi.

propositions.text: RPD found it more likely than not that the husband made no efforts to locate the Appellant based on evidence.
propositions.quote: Based on this evidence, the RPD found that it was more likely than not that the husband had made no efforts to locate her.

propositions.text: Court agrees with RPD's finding that husband likely made no efforts to locate Appellant; no rebuttal on appeal.
propositions.quote: My assessment of the evidence finds the same and I note that on appeal there is no rebuttal of this finding.

propositions.text: Appellant testified husband was searching; mother said unknown people asked about Appellant; no contact from adopted daughter or Aunt regarding husband.
propositions.quote: When asked by the RPD if her husband was searching for her, she testified that he had been. She stated that her mother told her some new people she did not know were asking about the Appellant, but she did not know who these people were and whether they were members of her husband's family. When asked if her adopted daughter (who is of adult age and lives in Kenya) had any contact with her husband, the Appellant stated "No, I don't think so." The Appellant was then asked if her Aunt, who provided a letter of support, has had any contact with anyone asking about the Appellant, and her response was she had not asked her Aunt but that she would not tell anybody, even if they asked about her. The Appellant similarly said her mom would also not reveal her whereabouts. No further evidence was adduced by the Appellant that any of her numerous siblings, who are still in Kenya, had any contact from her husband or had contact with persons asking about her whereabouts.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found husband likely made no efforts to locate Appellant; court agrees with no rebuttal; Appellant testified husband searched but no concrete evidence of contact.

propositions.text: No credible evidence husband sought Appellant or daughters in nearly four years since arrival in Canada.
propositions.quote: I note that it is nearing four years since the Appellant's arrival in Canada and there is no credible evidence that her husband has sought her whereabouts or the whereabouts of their two daughters who have remained in Kenya during this time.

propositions.text: Two affidavits dated 2016 note no contact from husband or his family seeking Appellant or children.
propositions.quote: Further, the Appellant's two supporting affidavits, which are both dated in XXXX 2016, note no contact from the Appellant's husband or his family for purposes of seeking the Appellant or her children.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no credible evidence husband sought Appellant or daughters in nearly four years; affidavits confirm no contact from husband or family.

propositions.text: Appellant testified husband could find her via mobile phone SIM card number which is traceable in Kenya.
propositions.quote: The Appellant testified that her husband could easily find her in the IFA locations because when you buy a SIM card for your mobile phone, there is a number provided which makes it easy to trace a person's whereabouts and asserted that there is no way to protect the privacy of your mobile phone number and location in Kenya.

propositions.text: RPD found no evidence or explanation how husband would get her cellphone number if she did not give it to him; lack of privacy does not mean husband can find number without it.
propositions.quote: The RPD observed that the Appellant had provided no evidence or any explanation as to how her husband would get her cellphone number if she did not give him the number, and that her explanation that there was no privacy in Kenya did not mean that there would be a way for her husband to find her cellphone number if she chose not to give it to him.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant testified husband could find her via mobile phone number; RPD found no evidence husband could get number without her giving it.

propositions.text: On appeal, argues it is not impossible to track someone via phone number; husband's family came to mother to find Appellant and daughters; RPD's statement is a travesty of justice.
propositions.quote: On appeal it is argued that in this day of the internet and cellphone that it is not impossible to track someone through their personal phone number. Other than this general assertion, no further argument or evidence is provided as to how the Appellant's husband would be able to accomplish this. It is further submitted that the Appellant testified that her husband's family had come to her mother in order to find out about the Appellant and her daughters. The Appellant further states that it seems to be a grave travesty of justice that the RPD stated that the Appellant's husband would not be able to get her cellphone if she did not give him the number.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues on appeal that tracking via phone number is possible; husband's family came to mother; RPD's statement is a travesty of justice.

propositions.text: Appellant's testimony did not indicate husband's family visited mother; mother said unknown people asked about Appellant but unsure if related to husband.
propositions.quote: First, I find that the Appellant's testimony did not indicate that her husband's family had visited her mother in Kenya looking for the Appellant and the daughters. The transcript of the RPD hearing clearly indicates that the Appellant's mother told her that some new people she did not know were asking about the Appellant, but that her mother did not know who these people were and whether they were members of her husband's family.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Appellant's testimony did not show husband's family visited mother; mother only said unknown people asked about Appellant.

propositions.text: No evidence how husband could track Appellant via phone number; Appellant not bound to use old phone or SIM card; RPD's statement not a travesty.
propositions.quote: Regarding the submission on appeal that it would not be impossible to track someone through their personal phone number, I observe that I have no further evidence before me as to how the Appellant's husband would be able to do so. Even if I were to accept that there may be some way for the Appellant to be located, for example through her old mobile phone number or SIM card, I find that the Appellant is not bound to use that phone or that particular SIM card in the future. The RPD observed that the Appellant provided no evidence or explanation regarding how her husband would be able to get her cellphone if she did not give him the number herself. I do not agree with the Appellant that this statement by the RPD is a travesty of justice.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no evidence husband could track Appellant via phone; Appellant not bound to old phone; RPD's statement not a travesty.

propositions.text: No credible evidence of mobile phone interception or surveillance placing Appellant at risk; no family contacted by husband; no unwanted contact since arrival in Canada.
propositions.quote: Aside from speculation that her husband could find her through her mobile phone, the Appellant did not provide credible objective evidence to establish mobile phone interception or surveillance that could place her at risk of harm. There is no evidence before me that any of the Appellant's family members, who remain in Kenya, have been contacted by her husband or members of her husband's family through their cell phones or any other means. I also observe that there is no evidence that the Appellant has received any unwanted contact from her husband on her cell phone or by other means since her arrival in Canada more than three and a half years ago. Therefore, on a balance of probabilities, I find that her husband would not be able to locate her through telecommunications, and a mobile phone specifically, if she were to return to Kenya.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no credible evidence of phone surveillance or contact by husband; no unwanted contact since arrival; husband unlikely to locate Appellant via phone.

propositions.text: RPD found Appellant's belief about school registry tracking speculative and unsupported by objective evidence; testimony inconsistent.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that there was no objective information which indicated how information about students was stored, whether information such as addresses were recorded, or its accessibility by members of the public. Accordingly, the RPD found that the Appellant's beliefs about being found through the school registry was speculative and not supported by any objective evidence. The RPD further noted that the Appellant's testimony regarding school registry documentation was in contrast to her earlier testimony that she did not need any documents, such as a birth certificate, to register her children in school.

propositions.text: Court notes findings not rebutted on appeal and sees no error.
propositions.quote: I observe on appeal that these findings are not rebutted, and I see no error here.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Appellant's belief about school registry tracking speculative and inconsistent; court sees no error and no rebuttal on appeal.

propositions.text: Country evidence shows FGM illegal but persists; prevalence varies by ethnic group; urban women less likely affected; state protection likely available.
propositions.quote: I considered the country documentary evidence which indicates that FGM is illegal in Kenya, but the practice continues with around 21% of women having undergone the procedure. It is performed mostly on girls between the ages of 12 and 18, but sometimes as young as seven. Prevalence is reported to vary across ethnic groups, but is highest amongst the Somali, Samburu, Kisii, and Maasai communities. Women/girls living in towns and cities are generally less likely to be subject to FGM than those living in rural areas. Further, objective documentation also indicates that the Kenyan government has made efforts to end FGM with various anti-FGM programs being run in partnership with international agencies and has successfully prosecuted a number of FGM practitioners. In addition, various Non-Governmental Organisations provide support and assist girls who wish to avoid undergoing FGM in obtaining protection. In general, the country documentation indicates state protection is likely to be available. And, if a woman/girl who is at real risk of FGM, or their accompanying family, is at risk of serious harm for opposing the procedure in their home area, they may be able to relocate to another area where they would not be at risk. I also considered evidence that the Kenyan government has made efforts to end the practice, including running various anti-FGM programs in partnership with international agencies. There have also been a number of successful prosecutions of persons performing FGM since 2011, when the FGM law was introduced, and Kenya's anti-FGM prosecution unit has deployed teams across the country in an attempt to prosecute more cases.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds FGM illegal but persists in Kenya; prevalence varies; urban women less affected; state protection and relocation options likely available.

propositions.text: FGM prevalence higher in rural areas and among uneducated women; Appellant not in high-risk profile; insufficient evidence of serious risk of forced FGM by husband in IFAs.
propositions.quote: I find that the country evidence indicates that the Appellant is not the profile of the group of women who have an elevated risk of being subjected to this practice, namely young, uneducated and residing in a rural environment. Thus, based on my assessment of the country documentation evidence, there is not sufficient evidence to demonstrate that the Appellant faces a serious possibility of persecution in the form of forced FGM by her husband in the IFAs.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Appellant not in high-risk group for FGM; insufficient evidence of serious risk of forced FGM by husband in IFAs.

propositions.text: NDP item 1.7 says Kenya's constitution and laws provide freedom of movement, generally respected.
propositions.quote: The National Documentation Package (NDP), item 1.7 suggests that the constitution and laws of Kenya provide for freedom of movement, and the government generally respects this in practice.

propositions.text: Kenya has large multiethnic cities like Mombasa and Nairobi where persons fleeing non-state actors may safely relocate.
propositions.quote: The documentation indicates that there are several very large, multilingual, multiethnic cities in Kenya, such as Mombasa (1.1 million) and Nairobi (3.9 million) where persons fleeing non-state actors may be able to safely relocate and establish themselves based on their own particular circumstances.

propositions.text: Many women live alone in Nairobi and single women can be employed depending on education level.
propositions.quote: The documentation also notes that there are significant numbers of women living alone in Nairobi and it is very possible for single women to be employed in the city depending on their level of education.

paragraphs.summary: NDP shows Kenya's constitution protects freedom of movement; large cities like Nairobi and Mombasa offer safe relocation and employment opportunities for women.

propositions.text: Gender-based persecution including domestic violence and FGM continue in Kenya but Appellant has not shown serious possibility of such persecution in IFAs.
propositions.quote: I note that gender-based persecution including domestic violence and FGM continue to be problems in Kenya, but find that the Appellant has not established that she faces a serious possibility of such persecution in the proposed IFAs on this basis.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds gender-based persecution continues in Kenya but Appellant has not shown serious risk in IFAs.

propositions.text: Appellant has not shown serious possibility of persecution or personal risk in Nairobi or Mombasa on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: Having considered all of the evidence, I find that the Appellant has not discharged her burden to show that she would face a serious possibility of persecution or would be subjected to a personal risk to life, risk of torture or risk of cruel and unusual punishment or treatment, on a balance of probabilities, in Nairobi or Mombasa.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes Appellant has not shown serious risk of persecution or personal harm in Nairobi or Mombasa.

propositions.text: RPD found Nairobi and Mombasa reasonable IFA locations; no undue hardship for Appellant to relocate there.
propositions.quote: The RPD considered the Claimant's personal circumstances and found that Nairobi and Mombasa were reasonable places to relocate to and that the Appellant would not face undue hardship in relocating there.

propositions.text: RPD guided by Federal Court of Appeal's Ranganathan decision setting high threshold for unreasonableness of IFA.
propositions.quote: In reaching this determination, the panel was guided by the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Ranganathan, which set a very high threshold for what makes an IFA unreasonable.

propositions.text: Courts require proof of adverse conditions jeopardizing life or safety to find IFA unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The courts have repeatedly outlined that the threshold requires, at a minimum, the proof of adverse conditions which would jeopardize the life or safety of the claimant in relocating, demonstrated based on actual and concrete evidence.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Nairobi and Mombasa reasonable IFAs; guided by Ranganathan's high threshold requiring proof of life or safety jeopardy to find IFA unreasonable.

propositions.text: RPD found no particular hardship identified by Appellant in relocating; concerns stemmed from belief husband could locate her.
propositions.quote: The RPD observed that the Appellant did not identify any particular hardship associated with relocating within Kenya, and her concerns about re-location stemmed from her belief that her husband would be able to locate her.

propositions.text: RPD considered psychological evidence including diagnosis and found Appellant could manage mental health in Kenya; reunion with daughters may improve symptoms.
propositions.quote: In its analysis of the reasonableness of the IFA locations, the RPD considered the psychological evidence which includes a diagnosis of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX as well as XXXX XXXX XXXX secondary to the separation from her daughters. The RPD found that the Appellant could continue with the management of her mental health in Kenya and that being re-united with her daughters may improve the symptoms related to her depression.

propositions.text: RPD noted many single and divorced women live alone in Nairobi; many women choose to live alone.
propositions.quote: In addition, the RPD considered the documentary evidence which indicated that there were a large number of single and divorced women living in Nairobi who have escaped gender-based violence and that many women choose to live alone.

propositions.text: Appellant previously lived and worked in Nairobi and established a business in a new community without family resources.
propositions.quote: Specifically, the Appellant testified that she had previously resided in Nairobi where she was gainfully employed. She was also able to successfully establish a business in a new Kenyan community with no family resources where she was able to support her family with little assistance from her husband.

propositions.text: RPD found it would not be unduly difficult for Appellant to establish herself in IFA locations.
propositions.quote: Based on all of the above, the RPD found that it would not be unduly difficult for the Appellant to similarly establish herself in one of the IFA locations.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found no hardship identified by Appellant; mental health manageable; many single women live alone; Appellant previously lived and worked in Nairobi; relocation not unduly difficult.

propositions.text: No specific arguments on appeal about RPD error in finding Nairobi or Mombasa reasonable IFAs.
propositions.quote: There are no specific arguments presented on appeal as to how or why the RPD erred in finding that the IFA locations of Nairobi or Mombasa were reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant presents no specific arguments on appeal about RPD's finding that Nairobi or Mombasa are reasonable IFAs.

propositions.text: New evidence includes Dr. XXXX's one-hour assessment report dated 2018 and letter explaining incomplete assessment.
propositions.quote: There is a report from Dr. XXXX XXXX, dated XXXX XXXX, 2018, which represents a one-hour assessment with the Appellant. Dr. XXXX indicates she has read the Appellant's BOC form, but she does not outline what other documentation, if any, was accessed to corroborate the self-reported information. The report observes that the Appellant had a prior psychological assessment conducted on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, but Dr. XXXX does not indicate if she had access to this earlier assessment. I also note that Dr. XXXX indicates that her report is focused on incidents that caused personal injury, but that she would comment on the Appellant's mental health. A letter from Dr. XXXX, also dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 explains that due to time constraints she was unable to complete an updated XXXX assessment.

propositions.text: Report describes domestic violence incidents, physical injuries, and mental health symptoms related to gender-based violence and refugee claim denial.
propositions.quote: Dr. XXXX report describes in some detail a number of specific incidents of domestic violence which the Appellant disclosed as being caused by her husband, and there are pictures of the Appellant's physical injuries. In the summary section of the report, Dr. XXXX opines that the Appellant bears physical signs and ongoing symptoms consistent with her experience of gender based violent including physical and verbal abuse in Kenya at the hands of her husband for refusing to undergo or let the children undergo FGM. Turning to the Appellant's mental health, Dr. XXXX notes that the Appellant's anxiety, depression and insomnia improved when she found work as a personal support worker with people with disabilities but that there has been a re-emergence of mental health symptoms due to her refugee claim being denied. It is reported that the Appellant has reduced her hours at work. It is recommended by Dr. XXXX that the Appellant would benefit from receiving on-going counselling and support and that her family doctor follow up with her for continued management of her mental health symptoms.

propositions.text: Dr. XXXX makes no recommendation on reasonableness of Appellant returning to Kenya.
propositions.quote: Dr. XXXX makes no specific recommendation related to the reasonableness of the Appellant returning to Kenya.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes new evidence from Dr. XXXX's one-hour assessment describing domestic violence, injuries, mental health, but no recommendation on return to Kenya.

propositions.text: Little weight given to Dr. XXXX's report on reasonableness of IFA; report focused on past injuries, minimal relevance to IFA assessment.
propositions.quote: I find that I can put little weight on the recent report from Dr. XXXX in relation to my analysis of the reasonableness of the IFA for the Appellant. The report itself represents a one-hour session which is primarily focused on a review and analysis of the Appellant's past physical injuries. This information is of minimal relevance to my assessment of the reasonableness of the IFA locations of Nairobi and Mombasa.

propositions.text: Report not a comprehensive psychological assessment; assessment instruments not detailed.
propositions.quote: Further, this report which is based on a one hour interview does not represent a comprehensive psychological assessment of the Appellant's mental health circumstances, and the measures or assessment instruments used to evaluate the Appellant's mental health are not detailed.

paragraphs.summary: Court gives little weight to Dr. XXXX's report on IFA reasonableness; report focused on past injuries and lacks comprehensive psychological assessment.

propositions.text: Appellant's mental health issues do not render IFA locations unreasonable; mental health services available in Nairobi and Mombasa.
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant's current mental health issues do not render the IFA locations unreasonable. There is country information that in Kenya, services such as mental health are available and accessible in the cities of Nairobi and Mombasa.

propositions.text: Government hospitals offer services to victims of gender-based violence including Gender Based Violence Recovery centres.
propositions.quote: Further, big government hospitals offer services to victims of gender based violence; they have "Gender Based Violence Recovery centres."

propositions.text: Appellant provided no evidence she would be unable to access mental health services in Kenya.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not provided any evidence to establish that she would be unable to access mental health services in Kenya.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Appellant's mental health issues do not make IFA unreasonable; mental health services and gender violence recovery centres available; no evidence of access issues.

propositions.text: The Appellant improved her education in Canada and secured employment, mitigating against IFAs in Kenya being unreasonable.
propositions.quote: the Appellant has improved her education in Canada by completing a diploma program as a XXXX XXXX XXXX.34 She has secured employment in this area in Canada

propositions.text: The Appellant managed mental health issues while completing education, supporting reasonableness of IFAs.
propositions.quote: The Appellant was able to complete this education successfully while also managing her mental health issues

propositions.text: The Appellant's improved profile will assist her in finding employment upon return to Kenya.
propositions.quote: the Appellant will be returning with an improved educational and work profile which will assist her in finding employment

propositions.text: The RPD noted the Appellant was gainfully employed in Kenya in another field.
propositions.quote: as noted by the RPD, the Appellant was gainfully employed in Kenya in another field

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant's improved education and employment in Canada, plus prior employment in Kenya, support reasonableness of IFAs in Kenya.

propositions.text: The burden is on the Appellant to show why the proposed IFA is not reasonable, not on the RAD to prove safety.
propositions.quote: the "burden does not fall on the RAD to explain why the proposed IFA would be safe" for the Appellant

propositions.text: The Appellant has not shown it is objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh to seek refuge in Nairobi or Mombasa.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not adduced evidence that demonstrates it is not objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh for her to seek refuge by relocating to and residing in Nairobi or Mombasa

propositions.text: The RAD agrees with the RPD that Nairobi or Mombasa are reasonable IFAs.
propositions.quote: I agree with the RPD that Nairobi or Mombasa are reasonable IFAs

propositions.text: An IFA is unreasonable only if conditions there jeopardize the Appellant's life or safety, which RAD did not find.
propositions.quote: In order for an IFA to be considered unreasonable, conditions in the proposed IFA would have to jeopardize the life or safety of the Appellant, and this is not the finding of the RAD

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Appellant must prove unreasonableness of IFAs; she failed, and RAD correctly found Nairobi or Mombasa reasonable IFAs.

propositions.text: Consideration of an IFA is determinative under sections 96 and 97 of IRPA.
propositions.quote: consideration of an IFA is determinative under sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA

propositions.text: The Appellant has a viable IFA in Kenya and is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: the Appellant has a viable IFA in her home country and as such, the Appellant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection

paragraphs.summary: The court finds IFA consideration determinative and concludes the Appellant is not a refugee or protected person due to viable IFA.

propositions.text: The RPD did not err on IFA availability and conducted a clear, well-reasoned analysis.
propositions.quote: the RPD did not err on the availability of an IFA, and its decision is correct. The RPD conducted a clear and well-reasoned IFA analysis

propositions.text: The Appellant failed to establish serious persecution risk or risk of cruel treatment if relocated to Nairobi or Mombasa.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution, or that she could be personally subjected to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture, if she relocated to Nairobi or Mombasa

propositions.text: The Appellant did not show relocation to Nairobi or Mombasa would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh.
propositions.quote: the Appellant did not establish that it would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh for her to relocate to Nairobi or Mombasa

propositions.text: This finding is determinative of the appeal.
propositions.quote: This finding is determinative of the appeal

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD's IFA analysis correct; the Appellant failed to prove persecution risk or unreasonableness of relocation, deciding the appeal.

propositions.text: The Appeal is dismissed and the RPD decision confirmed that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection under section 111(1)(a) IRPA.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the Appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision denying refugee or protected person status to the Appellant.
